en: And powder and shot were loaded onto the rhinos.
A pale-gray banner became their standard,
Their tumult split the sky,
And the uproar swelled ever louder.
Beside the army of heroic Kongurbay,
That mightiest of infidels,
The people of Kendeme stood
With Keng-Tung.
As for the Kalcha Kongurbay,
His spear was beyond all price,
And in that Kalcha’s host
There was nothing they did not possess.
Within his seething army
Were wrestlers of a thousand kinds;
Kongurbay’s warfare
Surpassed all the ages.
Among his champions
Were snarling infidels,
Heroes versed in the ways of the world;
His host was filled with mighty men,
With seers and giants,
The lords of Great Beijing.
There was black-bearded Dyngsha,
Who had studied occult arts,
And many formidable diviners;
There was an iron-rope net,
And Tegiz-Kanjarkolcho,
Whose every charge struck home;
Foot soldiers whom no swine could sate,
Who tore the life from men,
As though they would devour every giant they met,
As though they would finish everything at once,
And, if they bellowed, leave the world
In utter ruin.
What accursed creatures they were,
Riding mules and bearing spears!
Anyone who saw them recoiled;
The infidel’s champions,
His champions, were unlike any others.
Anyone who saw them recoiled;
Those rabid warriors
Had studied occult arts.
His seers and lions
Foretold the Altai-born torment
That was now to come.
He drove his seer forward,
And the seer examined
The valiant gray-wolf Choro.
Before Prince Kong, huge as a furnace—
The mighty prince known throughout the world—
Beside that great lord
Stood the Manchu khan Ezkara.
While all were standing in their places,
The seer came before them.
Bowing with frenzied reverence
And treading carefully where he stepped,
The seer entered, denouncing the boy
And recounting all he had seen:
“Prince Kong, lord of all the world,
Great and merciless sovereign!
Mightier than all the Khakan’s realm,
We have chosen to bring you a word,
Wondering, my khan, what may come of it;
We have prepared this counsel for you.
If this counsel is good,
Heed it and say, ‘Agreed.’
If this counsel is bad,
Then spare not one of our wretched lives—
Slaughter us all!
Our champion, our lion,
Do not walk into disaster.
Brave Kalcha hero,
Look closely at this accursed one
Whom you call your kinsman.
The stranger shows in his speech,
The outsider shows in his eyes.
Deceit is present in his words,
And distance is there in his gaze;
If this kinsman finds the strength,
He means to strike you down himself;
If this boy finds the means,
He means to cast you aside.
Can anyone from the Kyrgyz be your kin?
Can one who did not spring
From the farthest reaches of your China prosper?
Could this scoundrel from the Kyrgyz
Truly be your kinsman?
He will lay hands upon your treasure;
If this accursed Kyrgyz succeeds,
He will bring about your end.
Hero, will your coat of mail save you?
Heed my words, Kalcha:
Can one raised elsewhere be true kin?
Will a foreign coat ever fit you?
Can an outsider become your brother?
Double mail with lark-eye rings
Will not part when struck by a patterned spear;
This kinsman of yours who came from the Kyrgyz
Does not appear Chinese in form.
Mottled red and dun cloth
Will not part though we tear at every edge;
If by chance he falls into Chinese hands,
This man of yours does not look likely to flinch.
The armpit of double-linked mail
Will not part though we pull it wide;
This kinsman whom you so desire,
If he falls into Kalmyk hands,
Does not look likely to turn back.
If your kinsman is a trickster,
He will deceive you and wear your coat,
Then in the end bring calamity upon you.
This Kyrgyz has grown cunning;
Will he not keep calling himself my kinsman?
My true prince, think this over:
Will he not trick you out of your thoroughbred?
Once your thoroughbred falls into his hands,
Will he not drive you utterly mad?
If your kinsman is genuine,
Will he not still deceive you and wear your coat,
And drive your host downhill?
If your Kyrgyz survives,
He will turn his spear in his hand;
Once he learns the secrets of your camp,
He will destroy your settlement.
He will watch and learn your whereabouts;
If this Kyrgyz survives,
Will he not drive you all the way to Beijing?
If your kinsman learns your secrets,
Will he not raid and scatter your people?
By deceiving us, saying he has become kin,
Will he not settle his score in this way?
Your Kyrgyz will use honeyed words;
Do not let him deceive you into eating your food,
Coming here and saying, “I have become your kinsman,”
May he not contrive to cut off your head.
May he not sweep away your quiver;
If your Kyrgyz learns your secrets,
May he not overturn your baggage.
May his foal not eat from your tether;
If that madman begins to prance,
May he not threaten to slaughter your village!
May the sly Burut not surround and deceive you
And choose your stallion for himself;
May his Burut not drive everything away
And pursue us all the way to the Khakan’s realm.
May he not shoot down the stronghold’s defenders
And call it vengeance for his father.
May he not spear and slaughter the mighty,
Boasting until he is sated with blood.
May he not crush and rout your army
And somehow settle his account.
May he not start a senseless war,
Drive off your people, and slaughter them.
May your Algara, which you would never surrender if asked,
Never feel this Chinese people’s grim lasso!
There are six thousand Chinese san-kaldai;
If these Chinese grow angry,
May they not take your head with their swords.
His eyes are red as burning embers,
His cartridge pouch is filled with shots.
Think carefully, Kongurbay,
About this restless boy of yours:
My prince, he is no kin of yours at all.”
Thus the seer Ayar
Spoke in anguish.
The Kalcha stiffened in fury,
As though struck by God.
“I will make a slaughter now!” he cried,
Drawing his sword,
And summoned his forty princes.
At the cunning seer who had spoken,
The diviner esteemed by the people,
Who kept babbling on,
He bristled with rage,
Seized by violent fury.
The hair atop his head stood on end,
And the prince’s hair bristled at his nape;
Like a fierce black eagle,
He hunched in wrath.
His fury began terribly:
He slaughtered and cast down
Not the seers, but the khans.
“When my brother, lost among the Burut,
Had turned back and newly returned,
Had only just fallen into our hands,
Declaring that Burkan was God,
When he had only just arrived,
You raged while worshipping stones,
And stood there howling;
You sought to turn my brother
Into an enemy and corrupt him.
In the Kalcha’s old age,
It seems you wished to see my ruin;
You wished to separate
Younger brother from elder.
He became khan over the whole world,
And it seems you wished to behold
The white-bearded Manchu.
It seems you wanted, if you could,
To foster wicked arts;
You have roused, my seer,
The fury I have borne since ancient days.
You stand ready to make an enemy of my brother
And destroy him;
In my old age you stand ready
To make war upon my faith—
Upon my newly returned brother.
Damn you, seers!
From time immemorial
You have never ceased your trickery;
You speak evil words and never prosper.
Though our father Chilaba is one,
You speak of estrangement
And will not cease your mischief.
You make words blaze like fire,
And turn my brother into an enemy.
You make my own kin a foe,
And do this to me.
You meant to make my lament be sung,
You roaring seers,
And have worsened my wound.
By speaking such vicious words,
You meant to cost me my head.
You seers meant to question me
About some far-off youth of mine.
You meant to rot my treasure;
By committing this boundless deed,
Damn you, diviners,
You meant to bring about my end.
You mounted a swift horse to scout,
And by yelping on, you seers,
You meant to part me from my brother.”
Thus Kongurbay spoke,
Hunched in fury,
Bristling in distress.
As though darkness had fallen upon his wife,
Kongurbay capered wildly,
As though fleeing a pursuer.
He stiffened in wrath,
Looking ready to swallow them alive;
His eyes boiled in every direction,
And he gnashed those formidable teeth,
Chewing them side to side.
His eyes bulged from their sockets,
Huge as the bays of a lake;
Such was the accursed man’s bearing—
He seemed ready to swallow anyone he saw.
He stamped the earth in frenzy,
And the Kalcha hero began to speak.
When they saw Kongurbay’s wrath,
The forty tribes of China
And their vaunted lions
All wailed together,
Abandoning all hope of life.
Then Kongurbay, son of Alööke,
Let out a swine-like roar.
